categories.name: Unless / Without / Except
categories.description: Single negation indicators — negate the sufficient

questions.sentence: You will fail unless you study.
questions.correct: If you don't fail, then you studied.
questions.wrong: If you study, then you will not fail.
questions.explanation: "Unless" = negate the sufficient. "Fail" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Not fail → studied. If you didn't fail, then you must have studied. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: Without sunlight, plants wilt.
questions.correct: If no sunlight, then plants wilt.
questions.wrong: If sunlight, then plants do not wilt.
questions.explanation: "Without" = negate the sufficient. "Sunlight" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: No sunlight → plants wilt. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: Everyone is welcome unless they break the rules.
questions.correct: If someone is not welcome, then they broke the rules.
questions.wrong: If they break the rules, they are welcome.
questions.explanation: "Unless" = negate the sufficient. "Welcome" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Not welcome → broke the rules. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: The park is open except during storms.
questions.correct: If the park is not open, then there is a storm.
questions.wrong: If there is a storm, the park is open.
questions.explanation: "Except" = negate the sufficient. "Open" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Not open → storm. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: Without exercise, your health declines.
questions.correct: If no exercise, then your health declines.
questions.wrong: If you exercise, then your health improves.
questions.explanation: "Without" = negate the sufficient. "Exercise" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: No exercise → health declines. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: She won't apologize unless she is wrong.
questions.correct: If she apologizes, then she is wrong.
questions.wrong: If she is wrong, she will apologize.
questions.explanation: "Unless" = negate the sufficient. "Won't apologize" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Apologizes → she is wrong. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: The store is closed except on weekdays.
questions.correct: If the store is open, then it is a weekday.
questions.wrong: If it is a weekday, the store is closed.
questions.explanation: "Except" = negate the sufficient. "Closed" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Open → weekday. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: Without a map, hikers get lost.
questions.correct: If no map, then hikers get lost.
questions.wrong: If hikers have a map, then they do not get lost.
questions.explanation: "Without" = negate the sufficient. "Map" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: No map → hikers get lost. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: You will be fined unless you pay on time.
questions.correct: If you are not fined, then you paid on time.
questions.wrong: If you pay on time, you will be fined.
questions.explanation: "Unless" = negate the sufficient. "Fined" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Not fined → paid on time. If you weren't fined, then you must have paid on time. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: The dog stays inside except when it is sunny.
questions.correct: If the dog is outside, then it is sunny.
questions.wrong: If it is sunny, the dog stays inside.
questions.explanation: "Except" = negate the sufficient. "Stays inside" is in the sufficient position, so we negate it: Outside → sunny. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

categories.name: None / Cannot
categories.description: Single negation indicators — negate the necessary

questions.sentence: No doctor would recommend this treatment.
questions.correct: If someone is a doctor, then they would not recommend this treatment.
questions.wrong: Some doctors would recommend this treatment.
questions.explanation: "No" = negate the necessary. "Recommend this treatment" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Doctor → would NOT recommend this treatment. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: None of the applicants were qualified.
questions.correct: All applicants were not qualified.
questions.wrong: Some applicants were qualified.
questions.explanation: "None" = negate the necessary. "Qualified" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Applicant → NOT qualified. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: No student who cheats will pass.
questions.correct: If a student cheats, then they will not pass.
questions.wrong: Some students who cheat will pass.
questions.explanation: "No" = negate the necessary. "Pass" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Student who cheats → will NOT pass. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: Children cannot drive.
questions.correct: If someone is a child, then they cannot drive.
questions.wrong: Some children can drive.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" = negate the necessary. "Drive" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Child → canNOT drive. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: No one without a badge can enter the building.
questions.correct: If without a badge, then you cannot enter the building.
questions.wrong: If someone has a badge, they can enter the building.
questions.explanation: "No" = negate the necessary. "Enter the building" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Without a badge → canNOT enter the building. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: None of the cookies are sugar-free.
questions.correct: All cookies contain sugar.
questions.wrong: Some cookies are sugar-free.
questions.explanation: "None" = negate the necessary. "Sugar-free" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Cookie → NOT sugar-free. All cookies contain sugar. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: No one who litters cares about the environment.
questions.correct: If someone litters, then they do not care about the environment.
questions.wrong: Some people who litter care about the environment.
questions.explanation: "No" = negate the necessary. "Cares about the environment" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Litters → does NOT care about the environment. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: None of the flights were on time.
questions.correct: All flights were not on time.
questions.wrong: Some flights were on time.
questions.explanation: "None" = negate the necessary. "On time" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Flight → NOT on time. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: No healthy dessert contains artificial sweeteners.
questions.correct: If a dessert is healthy, then it does not contain artificial sweeteners.
questions.wrong: Some healthy desserts contain artificial sweeteners.
questions.explanation: "No" = negate the necessary. "Contains artificial sweeteners" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Healthy dessert → does NOT contain artificial sweeteners. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: Cats cannot fly.
questions.correct: If it is a cat, then it cannot fly.
questions.wrong: Some cats can fly.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" = negate the necessary. "Fly" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Cat → canNOT fly. (B) says the opposite.

categories.name: Combined: Cannot + Unless / Without
categories.description: Two negation indicators together acting as conditional triggers — negations cancel each other out. Note: 'without' only counts as a conditional trigger when it introduces a condition, NOT when it modifies a noun (e.g., 'No one without a badge' — here 'without' describes the person, so only 'no' is the indicator).

questions.sentence: You cannot vote unless you are registered.
questions.correct: If you voted, then you are registered.
questions.wrong: If you are registered, then you voted.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "unless" → the negations cancel. Vote → registered. If you voted, you must be registered. (B) goes in the wrong direction — being registered doesn't mean you voted.

questions.sentence: You cannot drive without a license.
questions.correct: If you drove, then you have a license.
questions.wrong: If you have a license, then you drove.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "without" → the negations cancel. Drive → have a license. If you drove, you must have a license. (B) goes in the wrong direction — having a license doesn't mean you drove.

questions.sentence: The machine cannot operate without electricity.
questions.correct: If the machine operates, then there is electricity.
questions.wrong: If there is electricity, the machine operates.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "without" → the negations cancel. Machine operates → electricity. If the machine is running, there must be electricity. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: You cannot pass the class unless you submit the final paper.
questions.correct: If you passed the class, then you submitted the final paper.
questions.wrong: If you submitted the final paper, then you passed the class.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "unless" → the negations cancel. Pass → submitted final paper. If you passed, you must have submitted it. (B) goes in the wrong direction — submitting doesn't guarantee passing.

questions.sentence: No one can compete without signing the waiver.
questions.correct: If someone competed, then they signed the waiver.
questions.wrong: If someone signed the waiver, then they competed.
questions.explanation: "No one can" + "without" → the negations cancel. Compete → signed waiver. If they competed, they must have signed it. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: You cannot board the plane unless you show your ID.
questions.correct: If you boarded the plane, then you showed your ID.
questions.wrong: If you showed your ID, then you boarded the plane.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "unless" → the negations cancel. Board → showed ID. If you boarded, you must have shown your ID. (B) goes in the wrong direction — showing ID doesn't guarantee boarding.

questions.sentence: The cake cannot be baked without flour.
questions.correct: If the cake was baked, then flour was used.
questions.wrong: If flour was used, then the cake was baked.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "without" → the negations cancel. Cake baked → flour used. If the cake was baked, flour must have been used. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: You cannot access the system unless you have a password.
questions.correct: If you accessed the system, then you have a password.
questions.wrong: If you have a password, then you accessed the system.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "unless" → the negations cancel. Access → have password. If you accessed the system, you must have a password. (B) goes in the wrong direction — having a password doesn't mean you accessed it.

questions.sentence: No employee can get a raise without a performance review.
questions.correct: If an employee got a raise, then they had a performance review.
questions.wrong: If an employee had a performance review, then they got a raise.
questions.explanation: "No...can" + "without" → the negations cancel. Got raise → had performance review. If they got a raise, they must have had a review. (B) goes in the wrong direction.

questions.sentence: You cannot graduate unless you complete the internship.
questions.correct: If you graduated, then you completed the internship.
questions.wrong: If you completed the internship, then you graduated.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" + "unless" → the negations cancel. Graduate → completed internship. If you graduated, you must have completed it. (B) goes in the wrong direction — completing the internship doesn't guarantee graduation.

categories.name: Few
categories.description: Few = some are AND most are not. Two pieces of information in one word.

questions.sentence: Few students enjoy homework.
questions.correct: Most students do not enjoy homework.
questions.wrong: No students enjoy homework.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some students enjoy homework, but most do not. (B) goes too far — "few" tells us some do enjoy it, so "no students" is wrong.

questions.sentence: Few restaurants in this town serve breakfast.
questions.correct: Most restaurants in this town do not serve breakfast.
questions.wrong: Most restaurants in this town serve breakfast.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some restaurants serve breakfast, but most do not. (B) flips it — "few" means most do NOT.

questions.sentence: Few politicians keep their promises.
questions.correct: Most politicians do not keep their promises.
questions.wrong: No politicians keep their promises.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some politicians keep their promises, but most do not. (B) goes too far — "few" tells us some do, so "no politicians" is wrong.

questions.sentence: Few movies this year were worth watching.
questions.correct: Some movies this year were worth watching.
questions.wrong: No movies this year were worth watching.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some movies were worth watching. (B) goes too far — "few" guarantees that at least some were, so "no movies" is wrong.

questions.sentence: Few applicants passed the screening.
questions.correct: Most applicants did not pass the screening.
questions.wrong: All applicants passed the screening.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some applicants passed, but most did not. (B) says the opposite — "all" contradicts "few."

questions.sentence: Few dogs dislike walks.
questions.correct: Most dogs do not dislike walks.
questions.wrong: No dogs dislike walks.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some dogs dislike walks, but most do not. (B) goes too far — "few" tells us some do dislike walks.

questions.sentence: Few people read the terms and conditions.
questions.correct: Most people do not read the terms and conditions.
questions.wrong: Most people read the terms and conditions.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some people read them, but most do not. (B) flips it — "few" means most do NOT.

questions.sentence: Few cities have reliable public transit.
questions.correct: Some cities have reliable public transit.
questions.wrong: No cities have reliable public transit.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some cities do have it. (B) goes too far — "few" guarantees at least some do.

questions.sentence: Few teachers assign homework over the holidays.
questions.correct: Most teachers do not assign homework over the holidays.
questions.wrong: All teachers assign homework over the holidays.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some teachers assign it, but most do not. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: Few desserts at this bakery are sugar-free.
questions.correct: Most desserts at this bakery are not sugar-free.
questions.wrong: No desserts at this bakery are sugar-free.
questions.explanation: "Few" = some are AND most are not. Some desserts are sugar-free, but most are not. (B) goes too far — "few" tells us some are.

categories.name: Many
categories.description: Many = some = at least one. It feels like a lot, but on the LSAT it only guarantees 'some.'

questions.sentence: Many athletes train twice a day.
questions.correct: At least one athlete trains twice a day.
questions.wrong: Most athletes train twice a day.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know at least one athlete trains twice a day. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Many tourists visit the museum.
questions.correct: Some tourists visit the museum.
questions.wrong: Most tourists visit the museum.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know some tourists visit. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Many companies offer remote work.
questions.correct: At least one company offers remote work.
questions.wrong: Most companies offer remote work.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know at least one company offers it. (B) goes too far — "many" does not tell us it's more than half.

questions.sentence: Many children prefer chocolate ice cream.
questions.correct: Some children prefer chocolate ice cream.
questions.wrong: All children prefer chocolate ice cream.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know some children prefer it. (B) goes way too far — "many" is nowhere near "all."

questions.sentence: Many drivers ignore the speed limit.
questions.correct: At least one driver ignores the speed limit.
questions.wrong: Most drivers ignore the speed limit.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know at least one driver ignores it. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Many homes in the area have solar panels.
questions.correct: Some homes in the area have solar panels.
questions.wrong: A majority of homes in the area have solar panels.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know some homes have them. (B) goes too far — "many" does not mean a majority.

questions.sentence: Many doctors recommend this supplement.
questions.correct: At least one doctor recommends this supplement.
questions.wrong: Most doctors recommend this supplement.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know at least one doctor recommends it. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Many songs on the album are about love.
questions.correct: Some songs on the album are about love.
questions.wrong: Most songs on the album are about love.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know some songs are about love. (B) goes too far — "many" does not tell us it's more than half.

questions.sentence: Many voters support the proposal.
questions.correct: At least one voter supports the proposal.
questions.wrong: The majority of voters support the proposal.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know at least one voter supports it. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee a majority.

questions.sentence: Many plants need direct sunlight.
questions.correct: Some plants need direct sunlight.
questions.wrong: Most plants need direct sunlight.
questions.explanation: "Many" = some = at least one. We know some plants need it. (B) goes too far — "many" does not guarantee more than 50%.

categories.name: Not All
categories.description: Not all = some are not = at least one is not. It tells us nothing about the majority.

questions.sentence: Not all birds can fly.
questions.correct: At least one bird cannot fly.
questions.wrong: No birds can fly.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one bird cannot fly. (B) goes way too far — "not all" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all students passed the test.
questions.correct: At least one student did not pass the test.
questions.wrong: Most students did not pass the test.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one student didn't pass. (B) goes too far — "not all" tells us nothing about whether most passed or not.

questions.sentence: Not every restaurant on this street is expensive.
questions.correct: At least one restaurant on this street is not expensive.
questions.wrong: No restaurants on this street are expensive.
questions.explanation: "Not every" = not all = at least one is not. At least one restaurant is not expensive. (B) goes way too far — "not every" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all medications have side effects.
questions.correct: At least one medication does not have side effects.
questions.wrong: No medications have side effects.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one medication doesn't have side effects. (B) goes way too far — "not all" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all politicians are dishonest.
questions.correct: At least one politician is not dishonest.
questions.wrong: Most politicians are not dishonest.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one politician is not dishonest. (B) goes too far — "not all" tells us nothing about the majority.

questions.sentence: Not every employee attended the meeting.
questions.correct: At least one employee did not attend the meeting.
questions.wrong: No employees attended the meeting.
questions.explanation: "Not every" = not all = at least one is not. At least one employee didn't attend. (B) goes way too far — "not every" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all roads lead to Rome.
questions.correct: At least one road does not lead to Rome.
questions.wrong: No roads lead to Rome.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one road doesn't lead to Rome. (B) goes way too far — "not all" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all coffee shops serve espresso.
questions.correct: At least one coffee shop does not serve espresso.
questions.wrong: Most coffee shops do not serve espresso.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one coffee shop doesn't serve espresso. (B) goes too far — "not all" tells us nothing about the majority.

questions.sentence: Not every celebrity is wealthy.
questions.correct: At least one celebrity is not wealthy.
questions.wrong: No celebrities are wealthy.
questions.explanation: "Not every" = not all = at least one is not. At least one celebrity is not wealthy. (B) goes way too far — "not every" does not mean "none."

questions.sentence: Not all experiments produce useful results.
questions.correct: At least one experiment does not produce useful results.
questions.wrong: No experiments produce useful results.
questions.explanation: "Not all" = some are not = at least one is not. At least one experiment doesn't produce useful results. (B) goes way too far — "not all" does not mean "none."

categories.name: Most
categories.description: Most = more than 50%. Not all, but more than half.

questions.sentence: Most employees prefer working from home.
questions.correct: More than half of employees prefer working from home.
questions.wrong: All employees prefer working from home.
questions.explanation: "Most" = more than 50%. More than half prefer it. (B) goes too far — "most" leaves room for some who don't.

questions.sentence: Most birds migrate south for the winter.
questions.correct: More than half of birds migrate south for the winter.
questions.wrong: Few birds migrate south for the winter.
questions.explanation: "Most" = more than 50%. More than half migrate. (B) says the opposite — "few" means most do NOT, which contradicts "most do."

questions.sentence: Most customers were satisfied with the service.
questions.correct: More than half of customers were satisfied.
questions.wrong: All customers were satisfied with the service.
questions.explanation: "Most" = more than 50%. More than half were satisfied. (B) goes too far — "most" is not "all."

questions.sentence: Most countries have a national anthem.
questions.correct: More than half of countries have a national anthem.
questions.wrong: Every country has a national anthem.
questions.explanation: "Most" = more than 50%. More than half have one. (B) goes too far — "most" does not mean "every."

questions.sentence: Most students in the class scored above 80.
questions.correct: More than half of the students scored above 80.
questions.wrong: Few students in the class scored above 80.
questions.explanation: "Most" = more than 50%. More than half scored above 80. (B) says the opposite — "few" means most did NOT score above 80, which contradicts the statement.

questions.sentence: The train usually arrives on time.
questions.correct: More than half of the time, the train arrives on time.
questions.wrong: The train always arrives on time.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = most = more than 50%. More than half the time it's on time. (B) goes too far — "usually" leaves room for exceptions.

questions.sentence: She usually walks to work.
questions.correct: More than half of the time, she walks to work.
questions.wrong: She always walks to work.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = most = more than 50%. More than half the time she walks. (B) goes too far — "usually" is not "always."

questions.sentence: It usually rains in April.
questions.correct: More than half of the time, it rains in April.
questions.wrong: It rains every day in April.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = most = more than 50%. It rains more than half the time. (B) goes too far — "usually" does not mean every day.

questions.sentence: The restaurant is usually crowded on weekends.
questions.correct: More than half of weekends, the restaurant is crowded.
questions.wrong: The restaurant is crowded every weekend.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = most = more than 50%. More than half of weekends it's crowded. (B) goes too far — "usually" leaves room for quiet weekends.

questions.sentence: He usually finishes his work before 5 PM.
questions.correct: More than half of the time, he finishes before 5 PM.
questions.wrong: He rarely finishes before 5 PM.
questions.explanation: "Usually" = most = more than 50%. More than half the time he finishes early. (B) says the opposite — "rarely" means most of the time he does NOT finish early.

questions.sentence: Experienced drivers are generally safer.
questions.correct: More than half of experienced drivers are safer.
questions.wrong: All experienced drivers are safer.
questions.explanation: "Generally" = most = more than 50%. More than half are safer. (B) goes too far — "generally" leaves room for exceptions.

questions.sentence: Organic produce is generally more expensive.
questions.correct: More than half of organic produce is more expensive.
questions.wrong: All organic produce is more expensive.
questions.explanation: "Generally" = most = more than 50%. More than half is more expensive. (B) goes too far — "generally" does not mean "all."

questions.sentence: People generally prefer warm weather.
questions.correct: More than half of people prefer warm weather.
questions.wrong: Everyone prefers warm weather.
questions.explanation: "Generally" = most = more than 50%. More than half prefer it. (B) goes too far — "generally" is not "everyone."

questions.sentence: Older buildings are generally less energy efficient.
questions.correct: More than half of older buildings are less energy efficient.
questions.wrong: Few older buildings are less energy efficient.
questions.explanation: "Generally" = most = more than 50%. More than half are less efficient. (B) says the opposite — "few" means most are NOT less efficient, which contradicts "generally."

questions.sentence: Students generally perform better with more sleep.
questions.correct: More than half of students perform better with more sleep.
questions.wrong: All students perform better with more sleep.
questions.explanation: "Generally" = most = more than 50%. More than half perform better. (B) goes too far — "generally" leaves room for exceptions.

categories.name: Some
categories.description: Some = at least one. Could be 1, could be all. We just know it's not zero.

questions.sentence: Some cats are friendly.
questions.correct: At least one cat is friendly.
questions.wrong: Most cats are friendly.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one cat is friendly. (B) goes too far — "some" doesn't tell us it's more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Some houses on this block have pools.
questions.correct: At least one house on this block has a pool.
questions.wrong: 6 houses on this block have pools.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one house has a pool, but we can't be sure it's 6. "Some" only guarantees at least one — not a specific number.

questions.sentence: Some employees received a bonus.
questions.correct: At least one employee received a bonus.
questions.wrong: Most employees received a bonus.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one got a bonus. (B) goes too far — "some" doesn't tell us it's more than half.

questions.sentence: Some books on the shelf are first editions.
questions.correct: At least one book on the shelf is a first edition.
questions.wrong: 5 books on the shelf are first editions.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one book is a first edition, but we can't be sure it's 5. "Some" only guarantees at least one — not a specific number.

questions.sentence: Some voters changed their minds.
questions.correct: At least one voter changed their mind.
questions.wrong: Most voters changed their minds.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one voter changed their mind. (B) goes too far — "some" doesn't tell us it's more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Some students in the class speak Spanish.
questions.correct: At least one student in the class speaks Spanish.
questions.wrong: 7 students in the class speak Spanish.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one student speaks Spanish, but we can't be sure it's 7. "Some" only guarantees at least one — not a specific number.

questions.sentence: Some of the paintings were damaged.
questions.correct: At least one painting was damaged.
questions.wrong: Most of the paintings were damaged.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one painting was damaged. (B) goes too far — "some" doesn't tell us it's more than half.

questions.sentence: Some parks in the city allow dogs.
questions.correct: At least one park in the city allows dogs.
questions.wrong: 4 parks in the city allow dogs.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one park allows dogs, but we can't be sure it's 4. "Some" only guarantees at least one — not a specific number.

questions.sentence: Some teachers use technology in the classroom.
questions.correct: At least one teacher uses technology in the classroom.
questions.wrong: Most teachers use technology in the classroom.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one teacher uses it. (B) goes too far — "some" doesn't tell us it's more than 50%.

questions.sentence: Some runners finished under three hours.
questions.correct: At least one runner finished under three hours.
questions.wrong: 8 runners finished under three hours.
questions.explanation: "Some" = at least one. We know at least one runner finished under three hours, but we can't be sure it's 8. "Some" only guarantees at least one — not a specific number.

questions.sentence: All mammals breathe air.
questions.correct: 100% of mammals breathe air.
questions.wrong: Some mammals do not breathe air.
questions.explanation: "All" = 100%. Every single mammal breathes air. (B) directly contradicts the statement — if all do, then none are excluded.

questions.sentence: Every passenger must wear a seatbelt.
questions.correct: No passenger is exempt from wearing a seatbelt.
questions.wrong: Some passengers do not have to wear a seatbelt.
questions.explanation: "Every" = all = 100%. No exceptions. (B) directly contradicts the statement — if every passenger must, then none are exempt.

questions.sentence: All submissions must be received by Friday.
questions.correct: 100% of submissions must be received by Friday.
questions.wrong: Some submissions do not have to be received by Friday.
questions.explanation: "All" = 100%. Every submission must be in by Friday. (B) directly contradicts the statement — if all must, then none are exempt.

questions.sentence: Every student who enrolls receives a textbook.
questions.correct: If a student enrolls, then they receive a textbook.
questions.wrong: Some students who enroll do not receive a textbook.
questions.explanation: "Every" = all = 100%. If you enroll, you get a textbook. (B) directly contradicts the statement — "every" means no one is left out.

questions.sentence: All visitors must sign in at the front desk.
questions.correct: 100% of the visitors sign in at the front desk.
questions.wrong: Some visitors do not sign in at the front desk.
questions.explanation: "All" = 100%. Every visitor must sign in. (B) directly contradicts the statement — if all must, then none are excluded.

categories.name: Nearly All
categories.description: Nearly all = at least most, close to 100% but not all.

questions.sentence: Nearly all the tickets were sold.
questions.correct: Most of the tickets were sold.
questions.wrong: All of the tickets were sold.
questions.explanation: "Nearly all" = at least most, close to 100%. We can say most were sold. (B) goes too far — "nearly" tells us it's not quite all.

questions.sentence: Nearly all students completed the assignment.
questions.correct: More than half of students completed the assignment.
questions.wrong: Every student completed the assignment.
questions.explanation: "Nearly all" = at least most, close to 100%. More than half completed it. (B) goes too far — "nearly all" is not "every."

questions.sentence: Nearly all the reviews were positive.
questions.correct: Most of the reviews were positive.
questions.wrong: All of the reviews were positive.
questions.explanation: "Nearly all" = at least most, close to 100%. Most were positive. (B) goes too far — "nearly" means not quite all.

questions.sentence: Nearly all participants finished the race.
questions.correct: Most participants finished the race.
questions.wrong: Few participants finished the race.
questions.explanation: "Nearly all" = at least most, close to 100%. Most finished. (B) says the opposite — "few" means most did NOT finish, which contradicts "nearly all."

questions.sentence: Nearly all the houses on this street have garages.
questions.correct: Most of the houses on this street have garages.
questions.wrong: 100% of the houses on this street have garages.
questions.explanation: "Nearly all" = at least most, close to 100%. Most have garages. (B) goes too far — "nearly all" is close to 100% but not there.

categories.name: Frequently
categories.description: Frequently = at least some. It's unclear whether it reaches 50%.

questions.sentence: She frequently visits her grandparents.
questions.correct: She visits her grandparents at least some of the time.
questions.wrong: She visits her grandparents most of the time.
questions.explanation: "Frequently" = at least some. We know she visits, but it's unclear if it's more than 50%. (B) goes too far — we can't be sure "frequently" reaches "most."

questions.sentence: This road frequently has traffic jams.
questions.correct: At least some of the time, this road has traffic jams.
questions.wrong: This road has traffic jams most of the time.
questions.explanation: "Frequently" = at least some. We know traffic jams happen, but it's unclear if it's more than half the time. (B) goes too far.

questions.sentence: He frequently forgets his keys.
questions.correct: He forgets his keys at least some of the time.
questions.wrong: He forgets his keys most of the time.
questions.explanation: "Frequently" = at least some. We know he forgets them sometimes, but it's unclear if it's more than 50%. (B) goes too far.

questions.sentence: Customers frequently complain about the wait time.
questions.correct: At least some customers complain about the wait time.
questions.wrong: Most customers complain about the wait time.
questions.explanation: "Frequently" = at least some. We know some customers complain, but it's unclear if it reaches more than half. (B) goes too far.

questions.sentence: The printer frequently malfunctions.
questions.correct: The printer malfunctions at least some of the time.
questions.wrong: The printer malfunctions every day.
questions.explanation: "Frequently" = at least some. We know it malfunctions sometimes. (B) goes way too far — "frequently" does not mean "every day."

categories.name: Always / Invariably / Inevitably
categories.description: Always = all = 100%. Every single time, no exceptions.

questions.sentence: She always arrives early to meetings.
questions.correct: 100% of the time, she arrives early to meetings.
questions.wrong: She sometimes does not arrive early to meetings.
questions.explanation: "Always" = 100%. Every single time she arrives early. (B) directly contradicts the statement — "always" means no exceptions.

questions.sentence: Traffic jams inevitably occur during rush hour.
questions.correct: During rush hour, 100% of the time traffic jams occur.
questions.wrong: Traffic jams only occur during rush hour.
questions.explanation: "Inevitably" = always = 100%. During rush hour, traffic jams will always occur. (B) goes wrong — the statement doesn't say traffic jams can't happen at other times, just that they always happen during rush hour.

questions.sentence: James invariably orders the same dish.
questions.correct: 100% of the time, James orders the same dish.
questions.wrong: James sometimes orders a different dish.
questions.explanation: "Invariably" = always = 100%. Every time he orders the same thing. (B) directly contradicts the statement — "invariably" means no exceptions.

questions.sentence: The sun always rises in the east.
questions.correct: 100% of the time, the sun rises in the east.
questions.wrong: The sun sometimes does not rise in the east.
questions.explanation: "Always" = 100%. Every single time. (B) directly contradicts the statement — "always" means no exceptions.

questions.sentence: Lisa always double-checks her work.
questions.correct: 100% of the time, Lisa double-checks her work.
questions.wrong: Lisa sometimes does not double-check her work.
questions.explanation: "Always" = 100%. Every time she checks. (B) directly contradicts the statement — "always" means no exceptions.

categories.name: Never
categories.description: Never = negate the necessary. Same pattern as no/none.

questions.sentence: Paul never eats breakfast.
questions.correct: If Paul is eating, it is not breakfast.
questions.wrong: Paul sometimes eats breakfast.
questions.explanation: "Never" = negate the necessary. "Eats breakfast" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Paul → does NOT eat breakfast. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: The library is never open on Sundays.
questions.correct: If it is the library, it is not open on Sundays.
questions.wrong: The library is open on some Sundays.
questions.explanation: "Never" = negate the necessary. "Open on Sundays" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Library → NOT open on Sundays. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: Maria never raises her hand in class.
questions.correct: If it is Maria, she does not raise her hand.
questions.wrong: Maria raises her hand in class most of the time.
questions.explanation: "Never" = negate the necessary. "Raises her hand" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Maria → does NOT raise her hand in class. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: My friends never travel during the winter.
questions.correct: If my friends are traveling, it is not winter.
questions.wrong: My friends sometimes travel during the winter.
questions.explanation: "Never" = negate the necessary. "Winter" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Friends traveling → NOT winter. If my friends are traveling, it's not winter. (B) says the opposite.

questions.sentence: The Route 9 bus never arrives late.
questions.correct: If the Route 9 bus arrives, it is not late.
questions.wrong: The Route 9 bus arrives late some of the time.
questions.explanation: "Never" = negate the necessary. "Arrives late" is in the necessary position, so we negate it: Route 9 bus → does NOT arrive late. (B) says the opposite.
